title: Why The Forgetting Curve Is Not As Useful As You Think
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick takes aim at one of the most widely circulated images in teacher training: Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve, routinely wheeled out by school leaders as the justification for retrieval practice. He grants the historical achievement — Ebbinghaus brought experimental rigour to memory research at a time when phrenology was still respectable — but argues the curve was built on nonsense syllables deliberately stripped of meaning, which is precisely what classroom learning is not. The piece then marshals a century of subsequent work against the decay model: Bartlett on memory as reconstruction, Ausubel on meaningful learning anchored in prior knowledge, McGeoch and Wickelgren on interference rather than decay, and Bjork's storage-versus-retrieval-strength distinction, which recasts forgetting as temporary inaccessibility rather than loss. Hendrick's central claim is that if forgetting is variable, context-dependent and semantic, then spacing the re-exposure of isolated facts is the wrong prescription. He frames the whole problem as a 'lethal mutation' of good research, arguing that a misapplied finding is worse for teachers than no finding at all. The practical payoff is a shift of emphasis from repetition to depth: retrieval that restructures and connects knowledge rather than merely refreshing it. A useful corrective for any school using Ebbinghaus as the opening slide of its CPD on memory.
points: Ebbinghaus's design worked by eliminating meaning, so its findings travel badly into classrooms where meaning is the whole point of what is being learned.
Hendrick's strongest move is replacing decay with interference: students fail to recall not because knowledge has evaporated but because competing material blocks retrieval.
Bjork's split between storage strength and retrieval strength reframes forgetting as inaccessibility, which is why effortful retrieval, not passive review, restores it.
The 'lethal mutation' framing is the transferable idea here — a half-understood research finding can do more damage in a training room than ignorance of it would.
Practical upshot for planning: spacing alone is inert unless what is spaced is elaborated, interleaved and connected to existing schemas.
quotes: I see a lot of training where school leaders/trainers use Ebbinghaus as a vehicle to talk about retrieval practice and while the basic premise is important and interesting, I don’t think it’s particularly useful for teachers. I mentioned this in a talk recently and someone asked me to explain it in more detail so here it is.

However, while these findings are often linked to retrieval practice in education, the connection is not as straightforward as some suggest. Ebbinghaus’ experiments focused on the passive memorization of meaningless syllables and primarily makes claims about memory decay, but memorising trigrams devoid of semantic content is not really how we learn in authentic learning environments.

The curve assumes a uniform rate of decay, but subsequent research suggests that forgetting is highly variable and context-dependent. For example, knowledge that is well-integrated into prior schemas is far more resistant to forgetting (Sweller, van Merriënboer, & Paas, 2011). This is why spaced repetition works best when combined with meaningful retrieval rather than rote exposure.

Frederic Bartlett's groundbreaking work Remembering (1932) demonstrated that memory functions not as exact reproduction but as an active reconstruction. His research revealed that when we remember, we don't simply retrieve perfectly preserved information; instead, we rebuild memories in ways that align with our existing understanding of the world.

John A. McGeoch (1932) argued that time itself does not cause forgetting; rather, new learning interferes with old learning, making some memories harder to retrieve. This explains why students struggle to recall concepts—not because they have decayed, but because similar information competes for retrieval.

One of the things I’m a little obsessed with is lethal mutations of good research. “A little knowledge is a dangerous thing” as Alexander Pope said and in many ways, a misapplication of research is worse than complete ignorance of it.
Retrieval does more than prevent forgetting; it actually restructures knowledge, making it more accessible and adaptable. The effectiveness of retrieval is not just about repetition, but about depth.
